pairs.source_text: procurasti mihi per quendam hominem immanissimo typho turgidum quosdam platonicorum libros ex graeca lingua in latinam versos.
pairs.question: Cuius sectae philosophorum libros, ex graeca lingua in latinam versos, homo quidam immani superbia turgidus Augustino legendos procuravit?
pairs.question_en: The books of which sect of philosophers, translated from Greek into Latin, did a certain man swollen with monstrous pride procure for Augustine to read?
pairs.derivation: The pivotal moment of Book 7: a man 'swollen with monstrous pride' provides Augustine certain books of the Platonists, translated from Greek into Latin ('quosdam platonicorum libros ex graeca lingua in latinam versos'). Anchored to Augustine + the proud benefactor; single answer (Platonicorum), supported verbatim. Closed-book: the 'libri Platonicorum' that turned Augustine toward an incorporeal God are a famous landmark of his biography.

pairs.source_text: procurasti mihi per quendam hominem immanissimo typho turgidum quosdam platonicorum libros ex graeca lingua in latinam versos.
pairs.question: Ex qua lingua in quam linguam versi erant illi platonicorum libri quos Augustinus legit?
pairs.question_en: From what language into what language had those books of the Platonists which Augustine read been translated?
pairs.derivation: Distinct fact from the same sentence: the Platonist books Augustine read were Latin translations from Greek ('ex graeca lingua in latinam versos'). Anchored to the libri Platonicorum; short, verifiable, supported verbatim. Closed-book: Augustine's reliance on Latin versions of the Platonists (he had little Greek) is a noted detail of his intellectual formation.

pairs.source_text: tu procurasti pervicaciae meae, qua obluctatus sum Vindiciano acuto seni et Nebridio adulescenti mirabilis animae, illi vehementer adfirmanti, huic cum dubitatione quidem aliqua sed tamen crebro dicenti non esse illam artem futura praevidendi.
pairs.question: Qui duo, senex acutus et adulescens mirabilis animae, Augustino adfirmabant non esse veram illam artem futura praevidendi?
pairs.question_en: Which two men, a shrewd old man and a young man of marvelous soul, affirmed to Augustine that the art of foretelling the future was not real?
pairs.derivation: Two named figures dissuaded Augustine from astrology: Vindicianus, the shrewd old man (vehemently), and Nebridius, the young man (with some hesitation) -- both saying 'non esse illam artem futura praevidendi.' Anchored to Augustine + the astrology question; the senex/adulescens descriptors mirror 'acuto seni' / 'adulescenti.' Two named answers, both required, supported verbatim. Closed-book: Augustine's rejection of astrology under Vindicianus and Nebridius is standard biography.

pairs.source_text: is ergo vir nomine Firminus, liberaliter institutus et excultus eloquio, cum me tamquam carissimum de quibusdam suis rebus, in quas saecularis spes eius intumuerat, consuleret, quid mihi secundum suas quas constellationes appellant videretur.
pairs.question: Quod erat nomen illius viri liberaliter instituti qui Augustinum, de astrologia iam dubitantem, de constellationibus suis consuluit?
pairs.question_en: What was the name of that liberally educated man who, when Augustine was already in doubt about astrology, consulted him about his horoscope (constellationes)?
pairs.derivation: The man whose case clinched Augustine's rejection of astrology is named: 'is ergo vir nomine Firminus, liberaliter institutus,' who consulted Augustine about his 'constellationes.' Anchored to Augustine + the astrology consultation; single-name answer, supported verbatim. Closed-book: Firminus is the named protagonist of the famous twin-birth anecdote in Confessions 7.

pairs.source_text: et non erunt vera, quia easdem litteras inspiciens eadem debuit dicere de Esau et de Iacob, sed non eadem utrique acciderunt. falsa ergo diceret aut, si vera diceret, non eadem diceret: at eadem inspiceret.
pairs.question: Quos geminos, eodem tempore natos sed non eadem fortuna usos, Augustinus contra astrologorum artem in exemplum adduxit?
pairs.question_en: Which twins, born at the same time but not enjoying the same fortune, did Augustine adduce as an example against the art of the astrologers?
pairs.derivation: Against astrology Augustine adduces the scriptural twins Esau and Jacob: one horoscope ('easdem litteras') ought to have predicted the same for both, yet 'non eadem utrique acciderunt.' Anchored to Augustine's argument against astrologers + the named twins; single answer (Esau et Iacob), supported verbatim. Closed-book: Esau and Jacob as twins of divergent fortune are universally known.

pairs.source_text: itaque avidissime arripui venerabilem stilum spiritus tui, et prae ceteris apostolum Paulum.
pairs.question: Quem apostolum Augustinus, lectis platonicorum libris, prae ceteris avidissime arripuit?
pairs.question_en: Which apostle did Augustine, after reading the books of the Platonists, eagerly take up above the rest?
pairs.derivation: After the Platonist books Augustine turns to Scripture and above all to Paul ('prae ceteris apostolum Paulum'). Anchored to Augustine + the sequence after the libri Platonicorum; single-name answer, supported verbatim. Closed-book: that Augustine moved from the Platonists to the epistles of Paul is a canonical step in his conversion narrative.

pairs.source_text: Alypius autem deum carne indutum ita putabat credi a catholicis ut praeter deum et carnem non esset in Christo, animam mentemque hominis non existimabat in eo praedicari. et quoniam bene persuasum tenebat ea quae de illo memoriae mandata sunt sine vitali et rationali creatura non fieri, ad ipsam christianam fidem pigrius movebatur. sed postea haereticorum apollinaristarum hunc errorem esse cognoscens catholicae fidei conlaetatus et contemperatus est.
pairs.question: Quorum haereticorum errorem hunc esse Alypius postea cognovit, qui animam mentemque hominis in Christo praedicari non existimaverat?
pairs.question_en: Of which heretics did Alypius later recognize this to be the error, he who had not thought that a human soul and mind were proclaimed in Christ?
pairs.derivation: Alypius had thought Christ was God clothed in flesh without a human soul and mind, an opinion he later recognized to be 'haereticorum apollinaristarum hunc errorem.' Anchored to Alypius + his christological view; single named answer (the Apollinarists), supported verbatim. Closed-book: the Apollinarian heresy (denying Christ a human soul) is a known doctrinal label, here attached by Augustine to Alypius.
